nodes.bodyText:
[Design Proposal] Adopt OpInfo in ONNX exporter testing
Objective
This doc introduces a mechanism to test onnx export based on sample inputs registered in OpInfo(https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/opinfos-in-pytorch-1-10/253), similar to how MPS master/test/test_mps.py and other components of pytorch are tested.
It provides test coverage on ops and dtypes previously unattainable with manually created test models, and makes test authoring much easier for torch.onnx developers.
We can leverage OpInfo to discover gaps in the exporter support, especially for ops with partial existing support.
Motivation
The current unit tests for the torch.onnx export process, mainly residing in test/onnx/test_pytorch_onnx_onnxruntime.py, are manually created when operator support is added in the form of various symbolic functions.
It is hard to create comprehensive tests for each op given the amount of ops we need to support. It has caused the exporter to assume support of ops for which it only has partial support on certain dtype / input combinations, leading to a degraded user experience and most recently complicated support for torchdynamo. (example #85316)
Fortunately, there exists a test generation mechanism in pytorch core which is OpInfo. (See https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/opinfos-in-pytorch-1-10/253). OpInfos are Python objects that describe operators and how to test them, and is it adopted by tests across PyTorch components like torchscript, mps, fx and others.
It greatly reduces the need for manually creating new tests for torch.onnx, and enables a simple test authoring experience that allows for a comprehensive op level coverage. You can read more about OpInfo following https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/opinfos-in-pytorch-1-10/253.
Design Considerations

The work for enabling tests for ops need to be relatively low cost and can be done incrementally.
Developers need to be able to skip flaky test and unexpected tests.
All opsets should be tested.

Assumptions and Dependencies

We assume OpInfo to continue to be the testing strategy across torch components. (The info instances are in torch.testing._internal.common_methods_invocations.op_db)
All tests in the op_info will be run on all torch.supported opsets
Models will only be tested in tracing mode. The unit tests OpInfo enables are op-level tests, which compliments existing scripting tests.
Only cpu models are tested.
Tests for different ops will be enable incrementally as errors are fixed.
Current manually created test models should continue to exist, but new ops and fixes should first enable OpInfo based tests and only add new test models to test/onnx/test_pytorch_onnx_onnxruntime.py when needed.

General Constraints

It is unclear if the scripting mode is supported, since the op being tested is exposed via OpInfo.

We should be reasonably confident with tracing only tests with OpInfo, because we are only testing for op support and not the graph capturing aspect with OpInfo.


Only ops that have OpInfos will be tested via this mechanism.

It is possible to contribute new OpInfo to pytorch testing core. Supplemental tests can also be created in what is done in MPS
At ~530 in count, the existing OpInfos cover enough ops torch.onnx cared about and can detect many errors in test that we previously don't have mechanism of detecting.


The OpInfo are created for torch ops (not aten ops)

They have a reasonable 1-to-1 correspondence and can pinpoint errors in particular symbolic functions in practice.



High-level System Architecture
A new test module adapting the MPS tests master/test/test_mps.py will be created for torch.onnx.
The module will contain (1) an allow list for enabling tests (2) skipping mechanism for skipping particular dtype/opset combinations for given ops (3) a mechanism to create models that contains ops provided by OpInfo, that are tracible by the torch.onnx exporter.
The proposed implementation (#86182) demonstrates the minimum effort needed to incrementally enable tests for ops: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/86182/files#diff-2b7b872470e6ee3ef37f450f9fade3e23edd211da1e0dcff29405ed1f35025fbR296-R354. As well as the ability it has to detect gaps in the conversion support.
Alternatives considered

Not use OpInfo. Depending on OpInfo means when new test samples are added to an OpInfo, there is a potentially for it breaking affected torch.onnx tests. This can make torch.onnx fail more frequently, but we want this behavior to discover gaps and to prevent bc breaking changes. The skip mechanism allows a change to circumvent particular tests.

Not using OpInfo however makes it much harder to improve op coverage and correctness, as shown in the torch op support matrix analysis (https://www.justinchuby.com/torch-onnx-op-matrix/). There are too many edge cases to create tests for from scratch. We should avoid this duplication of work.



cc @mruberry

Currently, we have a CI check that checks to see if a PR has the appropriate labels on it, and fails the check if the right label is missing.
Instead of making this be something that makes the CI appear to have failed, lets make two changes:

Modify the CI check to only share a comment reminding the user to add the appropriate CI (without reporting a failing check)
Update mergebot rules in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/.github/scripts/trymerge.py to 1) fail the merge if the PR is missing the required labels and 2) post a comment explaining that the merge was failed due to the missing label

Original customer request:

Can we make the "needs labels" signal not part of the actual CI signal? I use the GitHub green/red indicator to easily check if a PR succeeded CI or not, but lack of labels turns this into a fail and obscures the signal.

🐛 Describe the bug
BatcherIterDataPipe caches the output of __len__ if it's run with a sized datapipe as input:

  
    
      pytorch/torch/utils/data/datapipes/iter/grouping.py
    
    
        Lines 104 to 113
      in
      12dd877
    
  
  
    

        
          
           def __len__(self) -> int: 
        

        
          
               if self.length is not None: 
        

        
          
                   return self.length 
        

        
          
               if isinstance(self.datapipe, Sized): 
        

        
          
                   if self.drop_last: 
        

        
          
                       self.length = len(self.datapipe) // self.batch_size 
        

        
          
                   else: 
        

        
          
                       self.length = (len(self.datapipe) + self.batch_size - 1) // self.batch_size 
        

        
          
                   return self.length 
        

        
          
               raise TypeError("{} instance doesn't have valid length".format(type(self).__name__)) 
        
    
  


However, when one of the previous datapipes is a ShardingFilterIterDataPipe, the actual length is only known once apply_sharding has been called on the pipe. This means calling len(datapipe) at any point prior to apply_sharding results in a wrong length after sharding is applied.
Example
from torch.utils.data.datapipes.map import SequenceWrapper
from torch.utils.data.datapipes.iter import ShardingFilter, Batcher
from torch.utils.data.graph_settings import apply_sharding

dp = SequenceWrapper(range(100))  # len(dp) is 100
dp = ShardingFilter(dp)  # len(dp) is 100
dp = Batcher(dp, 8)    # len(dp) is 13
len(dp)        # <- the issue—this caches the length of `Batcher`.
apply_sharding(dp, num_of_instances=2, instance_id=0)  # len(dp) should be 7 now (50 samples per shard, makes 6 full batches and one of 2 samples)
print(len(dp))  # Prints 13 rather than 7.
This prints 13, which is wrong. Removing the call to len(dp) before apply_sharding leads to the correct result of 7.
Proposal
The fix should be very simple: Changing the __len__ implementation of Batcher so that it doesn't cache computed results anymore:
    def __len__(self) -> int:
        if isinstance(self.datapipe, Sized):
            if self.drop_last:
                length = len(self.datapipe) // self.batch_size
            else:
                length = (len(self.datapipe) + self.batch_size - 1) // self.batch_size
            return length
        raise TypeError("{} instance doesn't have valid length".format(type(self).__name__))

This tracks the follow-ups from my PR stack(s) for implementing composable FSDP.
High Priority

Investigate behavior around _apply() and whether pre- and post-_apply() hooks are needed/reasonable

Since composable FSDP requires use_orig_params=True and use_orig_params=True usually overrides nn.Module._apply() to expose the FlatParameters before _apply() and restore the original parameters after:

  
    
      pytorch/torch/distributed/fsdp/fully_sharded_data_parallel.py
    
    
        Lines 1605 to 1610
      in
      3c6bddc
    
  
  
    

        
          
           with ( 
        

        
          
               self._deregister_orig_params_ctx() 
        

        
          
               if self._use_orig_params 
        

        
          
               else contextlib.suppress() 
        

        
          
           ): 
        

        
          
               return super()._apply(*args, **kwargs) 
        
    
  


The reason for this is to allocate contiguous memory for each FlatParameter when performing .cuda() (or similar) instead of allocating memory per original parameter and requiring a separate allocation and write back.
One possibility is to enforce the device_id argument for composable FSDP so that FSDP initialization can ensure the sharded FlatParameter memory is allocated on GPU directly before setting the original parameters to be views into that memory.



Medium Priority

Define FSDP's contract for buffers (e.g. for ignored modules)
#87923 (comment)

🐛 Describe the bug
SyncBatchNorm runs slower with torch.channels_last_3d memory format ( DistributedDataParallel  multi-gpu training), even though channels last format is supposed to improve the performance on GPUs.

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/nn/modules/_functions.py#L107
it seems we only check for torch.channels_last (2D case), and if the data is in torch.channels_last_3d (3D) it always gets converted to contiguous(). Commenting those lines improves the speed.
the channels_last support  was introduced in #46906

inline bool batch_norm_use_channels_last_kernels(const at::Tensor& self) {

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Context
Recently in #86829 we added a CI check to ensure PRs have a label added to them (here's why).
When the label is missing, the CI fails and our bot will post a comment on the PR with instructions on how to add the label
Request
When the CI check passes, the bot should search for the comment it may have left earlier (about how to add a label) and delete that comment.
The code to search for any previous comments and delete them are already part of the bot (it uses them to keep the comment near the bottom of the PR), but currently it only deletes the comment if it's planning to post an updated comment instead.
Code pointers

I find that after applying GroupNorm (pytorch offical implementation) in my network, the effect will be significantly reduced. This happens in almost all types of networks, such as VAE, DDPM, GAN, and target detection. In particular, in a generative type of network, the final generated image is clearly more like an average of multiple batches of images.
Previously I thought it was a problem with the method itself, until I implemented a version myself based on the GroupNorm documentation in the torch.
class GroupNormCustom(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self, n_groups, num_channels, eps=1e-6, affine=True):
        super().__init__()
        self.n_groups = n_groups
        self.num_channels = num_channels
        self.eps = eps
        self.affine = affine
        if self.affine:
            self.weight = Parameter(torch.empty(num_channels))
            self.bias = Parameter(torch.empty(num_channels))
        else:
            self.register_parameter('weight', None)
            self.register_parameter('bias', None)

        self.reset_parameters()

    def reset_parameters(self) -> None:
        if self.affine:
            init.ones_(self.weight)
            init.zeros_(self.bias)

    def forward(self, x):
        b, c, h, w = x.shape
        x = x.permute(0, 2, 3, 1)
        x = x.reshape(b, h, w, self.n_groups, c // self.n_groups)  # (b, h, w, g, f) s.t. c = g * f
        var, mean = torch.var_mean(x, dim=[1, 2, 3], keepdim=True)
        # norm_x = (x - mean) * torch.rsqrt(var + self.eps)  # (b, h, w, g, f)
        norm_x = x.sub(mean).mul(torch.rsqrt(var + self.eps))
        norm_x = norm_x.flatten(start_dim=-2)  # (b, h, w, c)
        if self.affine:
            # norm_x = norm_x * self.weight + self.bias
            norm_x = norm_x.mul(self.weight[None, None, None]).add(self.bias[None, None, None])
        return norm_x.permute(0, 3, 1, 2)

It brings significant performance improvements. I don't think my implementation deviates from the official documentation, but the result is much better than the official implementation.
Since I have no experience with cuda programming, I don't know the details of the official implementation, can you please explain what it does using python style code?

🐛 Describe the bug
I am working with the PyTorch Geometric Core Team on pyg-lib, a cpp backend for PyTorch Geometric. As part of work on accelerating heterogeneous gnns we use a CUTLASS Grouped GEMM kernel to compute matrix multiplications in parallel. We expose this to the pytorch python interface with two forms.
def segment_matmul(inputs: Tensor, ptr: Tensor, other: Tensor) -> Tensor:
    r"""Performs dense-dense matrix multiplication according to segments along
    the first dimension of :obj:`inputs` as given by :obj:`ptr`, utilizing
    dedicated kernels that effectively parallelize over groups.

    .. code-block:: python

        inputs = torch.randn(8, 16)
        ptr = torch.tensor([0, 5, 8])
        other = torch.randn(2, 16, 32)

        out = pyg_lib.ops.segment_matmul(inputs, ptr, other)
        assert out.size() == (8, 32)
        assert out[0:5] == inputs[0:5] @ other[0]
        assert out[5:8] == inputs[5:8] @ other[1]

    Args:
        input (torch.Tensor): The left operand 2D matrix of shape
            :obj:`[N, K]`.
        ptr (torch.Tensor): Compressed vector of shape :obj:`[B + 1]`, holding
            the boundaries of segments.
            For best performance, given as a CPU tensor.
        other (torch.Tensor): The right operand 3D tensor of shape
            :obj:`[B, K, M]`.

    Returns:
        torch.Tensor: The 2D output matrix of shape :obj:`[N, M]`.
    """

and
def grouped_matmul(inputs: List[Tensor], others: List[Tensor]) -> List[Tensor]:
    r"""Performs dense-dense matrix multiplication according to groups,
    utilizing dedicated kernels that effectively parallelize over groups.

    .. code-block:: python

        inputs = [torch.randn(5, 16), torch.randn(3, 32)]
        others = [torch.randn(16, 32), torch.randn(32, 64)]

        outs = pyg_lib.ops.grouped_matmul(inputs, others)
        assert len(outs) == 2
        assert outs[0].size() == (5, 32)
        assert outs[0] == inputs[0] @ others[0]
        assert outs[1].size() == (3, 64)
        assert outs[1] == inputs[1] @ others[1]

    Args:
        inputs (List[torch.Tensor]): List of left operand 2D matrices of shapes
            :obj:`[N_i, K_i]`.
        others (List[torch.Tensor]): List of right operand 2D matrices of
            shapes :obj:`[K_i, M_i]`.

    Returns:
        List[torch.Tensor]: List of 2D output matrices of shapes

    """
